what_it_does: When a chip is manufactured, the circuit pattern must be etched onto silicon by shining light through a physical mask — a glass plate with opaque and transparent regions. Because the features are far smaller than the wavelength of light, the pattern blurs and distorts unless the mask is pre-distorted in a clever compensating way; computing that pre-distortion is called Inverse Lithography Technology (ILT). ILT traditionally requires running expensive physics simulations hundreds of times to iteratively adjust each tiny pixel of the mask. SSDL-ILT trains a deep-learning model to output a corrected mask directly in one pass, skipping most of that costly iteration. Crucially, it uses self-supervised learning — it generates its own training signal from the physics of the lithography process rather than requiring a library of human-labeled mask examples — and it also automatically places tiny helper features (called sub-resolution assist features, or SRAFs) that improve the printed pattern without appearing in the final chip.
